title: Social Movements & Protest
hook: When ordinary channels fail or move too slowly, people organize and take to the streets. Social movements are how the unrepresented push change onto the agenda.
key_points: A social movement is sustained, organized collective action pushing for (or resisting) change.
Protest is a key tactic: making grievances visible and costly to ignore.
Movements have driven major reforms — civil rights, suffrage, labor, and more.
They work outside formal institutions, complementing elections, parties, and lobbying.
content_html: Formal channels — voting, parties, lobbying — are not the only way people shape politics, and sometimes they are blocked, slow, or closed to particular groups. Social movements are the answer that arises from below: sustained, organized collective action by people seeking to bring about, or resist, social or political change. Unlike a one-off rally, a movement persists over time, building shared identity, networks, and strategy. Protest — marches, strikes, sit-ins, boycotts — is one of its signature tactics, a way of making a grievance visible and costly enough that decision-makers can no longer simply ignore it.
extra_html: Movements matter because much of the change later treated as obvious began outside the institutions of power and had to be forced onto the agenda. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that movements for civil rights, the expansion of the vote, labor protections, and many other causes reshaped law and norms despite initially lacking formal political power. Their distinctive role is to operate alongside and outside formal institutions: where an interest group lobbies officials directly and a party contests elections, a movement mobilizes large numbers of people to shift public opinion and pressure the whole system. They are not always successful, and their methods and aims are themselves often contested. But the freedom to assemble, organize, and protest is closely tied to free expression, and the capacity for collective action gives those with little formal power a way to be heard — which is why the room a state leaves for protest is another measure of how open its politics really are.

related.title: Interest Groups & Lobbying
related.hook: Between elections, organized groups press their case to government every day. Lobbying is how that pressure is applied — and it's both a feature and a worry of democracy.

related.title: Freedom of Expression
related.hook: The freedom to speak, publish, and dissent is often called the first freedom — because without it, citizens can't check power or argue their way to better decisions.

related.title: Equality & Minority Rights
related.hook: Majority rule can become majority tyranny. Equality before the law and minority rights are how democracies stop the many from trampling the few.

flashcards.back_html: Sustained, organized collective action by people pushing for — or resisting — social or political change, usually outside formal institutions.

flashcards.prompt: How do social movements differ from voting or lobbying?

choices.text: They act largely outside formal institutions, often through mass mobilization and protest
They are run by the government itself
They replace the need for any laws

flashcards.explanation_html: Movements work through collective mobilization rather than the formal channels of elections, parties, or registered lobbying.

flashcards.prompt: What is the main point of protest as a tactic?

choices.text: To make a grievance visible and costly to ignore

flashcards.explanation_html: Protest dramatizes a demand and raises the cost of inaction, pressuring decision-makers and shifting public attention.
